newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco presses for end to garbage strike.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco presses for end to garbage strike.

text.p: San Francisco officials pressed Friday for a solution to a two-day garbage collectors' strike as trash piled up at homes across the city.
Mayor Willie Brown said he may declare a public health emergency by the end of the day if the labor dispute is not resolved. An emergency would allow Brown to call out city workers to pick up trash.
"The emergency has to be based upon the threat to public safety and the threat to the health of the people of the city and county of San Francisco," Brown told a news conference.

Management and union leaders made some progress in nine hours of talks at City Hall Thursday but disagreed on several issues, city officials said. Brown asked both sides to resume negotiations in his office later Friday.

Union leaders called the strike Thursday morning after workers rejected the latest contract offer by Sunset Scavenger Co. and Golden Gate Disposal & Recycling Co., subsidiaries of Norcal Waste Systems Inc., which collect the city's garbage.

The garbage collectors' strike, the city's first in 57 years, involved more than 500 employees who have worked without a contract since Dec. 31. Union officials said the workers would stay off the job for as long as necessary.
Norcal managers were collecting garbage from hospitals, hotels and large commercial clients Friday, city officials said. But garbage was piling up at homes.
City workers were combing the streets for garbage "hot spots" that might pose a health risk. The city advised residents not to put garbage out on the curb for the next 48 hours.

Workers are seeking a three-year contract, an 80-cents-per-hour pay increase, an early retirement plan and improved health benefits. The average garbage truck driver now earns $20.58 per hour or $49,000 a year.

Norcal said its latest proposal to striking workers would boost their pay by 13.3 percent over five years, and increase health care and pension benefits. "We can't afford to put anything else on the table," Norcal president Michael Sangiacomo said.
